title: FACIAL CLEFTING, OBLIQUE, 1
alt_titles: OCULOMAXILLOFACIAL DYSPLASIA WITH OBLIQUE FACIAL CLEFTS

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that oblique facial clefting-1 (OBLFC1) is caused by loss-of-function mutation in the SPECC1L gene.

checks.claim: Oblique facial clefting-1 (OBLFC1) is caused by loss-of-function mutation in the SPECC1L gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We show that loss-of-function mutations in SPECC1L are pathogenic for this human developmental disorder
checks.explanation: The abstract says LOF SPECC1L mutations are pathogenic for oblique facial clefts (ObFC).

paragraphs.text: Oblique facial clefts are a rare and distinctive class of facial malformations, corresponding to types 2 to 6 of the Tessier classification of facial clefts (Tessier, 1976; Richieri-Costa and Gorlin, 1994). Richieri-Costa and Gorlin (1994) suggested that the pattern of facial involvement could represent, in some instances, an oculomaxillofacial dysostosis. Saadi et al. (2011) showed that loss-of-function mutations in SPECC1L, a cytoskeletal protein, cause oblique facial clefting.

paragraphs.text: Tessier (1976) proposed an anatomic classification of facial, craniofacial, and laterofacial clefts based on personal observations, using the orbit as the primary structure of reference and differentiating 15 locations for clefts. Richieri-Costa and Gorlin (1994) noted that oblique facial clefts include types 2 to 6 of the Tessier classification.

paragraphs.text: Richieri-Costa and Gorlin (1994) reported 4 Brazilian patients with oblique facial clefts and a strikingly similar facial appearance; 3 of them had consanguineous parents. The authors suggested that the pattern of facial involvement and the entire clinical picture indicated a unique dysmorphogenetic process that could represent, in some instances, an oculomaxillofacial dysostosis. They considered the findings to be evidence for clinical variability and genetic heterogeneity.

paragraphs.text: In a girl with bilateral oblique facial clefts, Dasouki et al. (1988) found a de novo balanced translocation between chromosomes 1 and 22 on peripheral blood karyotype. They noted that a submicroscopic imbalance secondary to the translocation could not be ruled out, and recommended that chromosome studies be performed in children with such rare malformations.

paragraphs.text: Saadi et al. (2011) showed that loss-of-function mutations in the SPECC1L gene are pathogenic for oblique facial clefting. In mammalian cells, SPECC1L colocalized with both tubulin and actin, and SPECC1L deficiency resulted in defective actin-cytoskeleton reorganization as well as abnormal cell adhesion and migration. The authors concluded that SPECC1L functions in actin-cytoskeleton reorganization and is required for proper facial morphogenesis.

paragraphs.text: Saadi et al. (2011) found that during murine embryogenesis, Specc1l is expressed in cell populations of the developing facial primordia, which proliferate and fuse to form the face. In zebrafish, knockdown of a SPECC1L homolog produced a faceless phenotype with loss of jaw and facial structures. In Drosophila, knockdown phenocopied mutants in the integrin signaling pathway that show cell migration and adhesion defects.
